items.stem: A stratified random sample of size 50 is to be allocated by Neyman allocation between two strata with N₁ = 150, N₂ = 350, S₁ = 2 and S₂ = 2. The number of units to be selected from stratum 2 is
items.explanation: Neyman (optimum, equal-cost) allocation takes nₕ = n·NₕSₕ/ΣNₕSₕ. Here N₁S₁ = 300 and N₂S₂ = 700, total 1000, so n₂ = 50 × 700/1000 = 35. Trap: proportional allocation (nₕ ∝ Nₕ) gives 35; it agrees with Neyman only when S₁ = S₂.

items.stem: Lahiri's method is used to draw a sample with probability proportional to size, with replacement, from N = 5 units with sizes X = (2, 5, 3, 8, 2). The probability that unit 4 is selected at any given draw is
items.explanation: Lahiri's method picks a unit at random (probability 1/N) and a number between 1 and M = max Xⱼ = 8; it accepts the unit if the number is at most its size, otherwise it tries again. Each trial accepts unit i with probability Xᵢ/(NM), so after the repeats P(unit i) = Xᵢ/ΣXⱼ = 8/20 = 0.4, exactly PPS. Trap: Xᵢ/(NM) = 0.2 is the chance of accepting unit 4 on one trial, not on a completed draw.

items.stem: Match LIST-I with LIST-II. LIST-I (methods): A. Simple random sampling; B. Stratified random sampling; C. Cluster sampling; D. Sampling with varying probabilities (PPS). LIST-II (when used / key feature): I. Homogeneous population; II. Units of very different sizes, giving larger units more weight; III. No list of elementary units is available; IV. Heterogeneous population that splits into homogeneous groups. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Link each method to the situation it is designed for: Simple random sampling → Homogeneous population; Stratified random sampling → Heterogeneous population that splits into homogeneous groups; Cluster sampling → No list of elementary units is available; Sampling with varying probabilities (PPS) → Units of very different sizes, giving larger units more weight. So the matching is A-I, B-IV, C-III, D-II. Trap: each item of LIST-II is used exactly once, so fix the pairs you are sure of first.
